case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff’s voluntary dismissal without prejudice under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i) qualifies as a “final judgment, order, or proceeding” that a district court may reopen under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b) (relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding”) in interaction with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i) (plaintiff’s unilateral notice of dismissal without a court order).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) voluntary dismissal without prejudice is a “final ... proceeding” within the meaning of Rule 60(b), so the district court retains power to grant post-dismissal relief on just terms when extraordinary circumstances arise. He emphasizes that Rule 60(b) is written to reach not only judgments and orders but also “proceedings,” a broader term that can encompass a party-initiated dismissal that terminates the federal case. He also relies on historical practice and the ‘transplanted’ meaning of “proceeding” from predecessor remedial regimes, which were understood to allow courts to set aside voluntary dismissals in appropriate circumstances. On the facts, he contends that arbitration irregularities and subsequent legal developments affecting arbitration-related federal jurisdiction (citing Badgerow) created inequity that warranted reopening under Rule 60(b).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal without prejudice is self-executing and is not a “final judgment” or “order” because it involves no judicial action, and it is not the sort of ‘final’ disposition covered by Rule 60(b) because it leaves the plaintiff free to refile. Under this view, once the notice is filed the case is terminated and the district court lacks jurisdiction to ‘reopen’ it via Rule 60(b) because there is nothing judicial to set aside. Respondent characterizes the issue as a narrow, rarely recurring procedural question and maintains the Tenth Circuit correctly held that Rule 60(b) relief is unavailable in these circumstances.
key_precedents: Badgerow v. Walters (U.S. Supreme Court) (referenced regarding arbitration-related jurisdiction and alleged intervening change in law)
Volt Information Sciences, Inc. v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University (U.S. Supreme Court) (party autonomy to structure arbitration procedures)
Stolt-Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds International Corp. (U.S. Supreme Court) (arbitrator authority derives from party agreement)
Mid Atl. Capital Corp. v. Bien (10th Cir.) (contracting for explained arbitration awards)
Hall v. Hall (U.S. Supreme Court) (interpretive principle about transplanted legal terms carrying their historical meaning)
Palace Hardware Co. v. Smith (Cal. Supreme Court) (historical authority cited for setting aside a voluntary dismissal)
Lusas v. St. Patrick’s Roman Catholic Church Corp. (historical authority cited on setting aside dismissals)
Salazar v. Steelman (Cal. Ct. App.) (historical authority affirming reinstatement after voluntary dismissal)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s structural concern—that Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) is self-executing and should not invite continuing judicial “supervision”—is the best argument on the other side, but it is ultimately answered by the text Rule 60(b) chose: relief may be granted from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding.” As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading “proceeding” to require a judicial act collapses it into “judgment” and “order” and creates surplusage; a notice that terminates the case on filing is naturally a final federal “proceeding” in the only relevant sense (the district court’s involvement is over). Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term principle reinforces that this remedial language should be read against historical practice allowing narrow equitable set-aside of voluntary terminations, while the “without prejudice” label goes to preclusion, not whether the federal proceeding has ended. Consistent with minimalism and institutional legitimacy, I would hold only that Rule 60(b) authority exists to entertain the motion and remand for application of the demanding standards, which addresses Kavanaugh’s floodgates/workability worry without rewriting the Rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument is Justice Kavanaugh’s structural concern that a self-executing Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice leaves no judicial act for Rule 60(b) to undo, but that cannot overcome Rule 60(b)’s text authorizing relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, reading “proceeding” to require a court-entered disposition collapses it into “judgment” and “order” and violates ordinary interpretive rules against surplusage; a filed notice that conclusively ends the federal case is naturally a “final … proceeding” even if “without prejudice” affects only preclusion. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term principle, invoked by Roberts, reinforces that we should read this remedial term against the historical scope of equitable set-aside authority rather than invent an atextual judicial-act prerequisite. Workability concerns are adequately handled by Rule 60(b)’s demanding, exceptional-grounds standard, not by rewriting the Rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Kavanaugh’s structural/workability argument that a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice is self-executing and should leave no residue of judicial power for Rule 60(b) to operate upon. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, Rule 60(b)’s text reaches a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and importing a judicial-act prerequisite effectively reads “proceeding” out of the Rule as surplusage; a docketed notice that terminates the federal case is “final” in the practical sense that the court’s involvement ends unless extraordinary relief is warranted. Hall v. Hall, which Roberts invokes, reinforces that we should carry forward the traditional remedial understanding of these transplanted terms rather than impose atextual limitations based on modern structural intuitions. And the floodgates concern is adequately addressed, as Roberts and Kagan suggest, by insisting that Rule 60(b)’s demanding standards—especially the “extraordinary circumstances” framework—remain a narrow safety valve that preserves Rule 41’s immediacy as the norm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed as a structural/workability concern that Rule 60(b) would become a roving supervisory power over a self-executing Rule 41 notice—cannot overcome the Rule’s text authorizing relief from a “final … proceeding,” and, as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, importing a judicial-act requirement would render “proceeding” largely surplusage beside “judgment” and “order.” Justice Kavanaugh’s remaining worry is better handled, as Roberts proposes, by a narrow holding recognizing authority and remanding for the demanding “extraordinary circumstances” inquiry, which preserves Rule 41’s immediacy while keeping a safety valve for serious unfairness—especially where vulnerable litigants are harmed by mistake, misconduct, or confusion. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term principle, cited by Roberts and Thomas, reinforces reading this remedial phrase against historical equitable practice rather than narrowing it based on policy fears. The “without prejudice” label affects preclusion, not the finality of the federal proceeding, so it does not defeat Rule 60(b) jurisdiction to consider limited relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Kavanaugh’s structural worry that Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) is self-executing and Rule 60(b) should not become a continuing supervisory power, but that concern cannot justify an atextual judicial-act limitation. As Chief Justice Roberts frames it, the workable middle is to acknowledge Rule 60(b) authority while letting its demanding, extraordinary-grounds standards do the cabining work—preserving Rule 41’s immediacy in ordinary cases. Justice Thomas’s surplusage argument remains decisive for me as a textualist: if “proceeding” is confined to court-entered dispositions, it collapses into “judgment” and “order,” whereas a docketed notice that ends the federal case fits ordinary usage of a “final … proceeding.” Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term logic, invoked by Roberts and Gorsuch, reinforces reading this remedial language against historical practice of limited set-aside rather than narrowing it by implied structural constraints.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point, pressed by Justice Kavanaugh earlier, is structural: Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) is self-executing, so allowing Rule 60(b) review risks an amorphous, continuing supervisory power. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, Rule 60(b)’s text reaches a final “judgment, order, or proceeding,” and imposing a judicial-act prerequisite would collapse “proceeding” into “judgment” and “order,” violating ordinary surplusage canons and the remedial breadth reflected in Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term logic. Kokkonen and similar cases don’t compel the respondent’s limitation; they underscore that jurisdiction and reopening are exceptional, a constraint already supplied by Rule 60(b)’s demanding standards rather than an atextual categorical bar. I therefore remain persuaded that a docketed notice that terminates the federal case is a final “proceeding” from which limited Rule 60(b) relief may be sought, with the merits properly addressed on remand under the Rule’s high threshold.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument remains the structural one I raised earlier: a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice is self-executing and should not invite continuing judicial supervision. But Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point—that Rule 60(b) expressly reaches a “final judgment, order, or proceeding”—together with Justice Thomas’s surplusage critique makes it hard, as a matter of ordinary meaning and rule-structure, to impose a categorical judicial-act prerequisite without effectively reading “proceeding” out of the Rule. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term principle, invoked by Roberts and Gorsuch, strengthens that conclusion by counseling that this remedial term carries forward historically understood equitable set-aside power for certain voluntary terminations, and the demanding Rule 60(b) standards sufficiently cabin institutional and workability concerns. On that limited ground, I would hold only that authority exists and remand for the merits inquiry, without suggesting routine reopening of Rule 41 dismissals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side argument is Justice Kavanaugh’s structural point that a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice is self-executing and involves no judicial act, so Rule 60(b) should not apply; but that limitation cannot be reconciled with Rule 60(b)’s text authorizing relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding.” As Justice Thomas (and the Chief Justice) emphasizes, importing a judicial-act prerequisite collapses “proceeding” into “judgment” and “order,” violating the anti-surplusage canon and effectively rewriting the Rule. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term logic, invoked by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, supports reading this remedial language against its historical equitable backdrop rather than narrowing it to court-entered decrees absent textual direction. Kavanaugh’s residual workability concern is adequately addressed by Rule 60(b)’s demanding, historically rooted standards, which preserve Rule 41’s immediate effect while allowing only exceptional reopening.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument is the structural/workability claim that Rule 41’s self-executing notice must categorically terminate judicial power, but that concern cannot justify reading a judicial-act requirement into Rule 60(b)’s express authorization of relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, restricting “proceeding” to court-entered dispositions collapses it into “judgment” or “order,” creating surplusage and a procedural trap where equitable relief depends on whether termination occurred by notice or by court order. Justice Kavanaugh’s lingering institutional worry is addressed by the narrowness of Rule 60(b)’s extraordinary-relief standards, which preserve Rule 41’s immediate effect while providing a limited fairness backstop in truly exceptional cases. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term logic, as invoked by Roberts and Kagan, reinforces that we should read this remedial language against historical practice rather than impose an atextual categorical bar.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(b) by its terms authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice—though self-executing and without judicial action—nonetheless finally terminates the federal case as a procedural matter, making it a “final … proceeding” eligible for limited reopening. Consistent with judicial minimalism, I would decide only that Rule 60(b) power exists in this posture, leaving the merits and the demanding “extraordinary circumstances” showing to the district court on remand. Hall v. Hall supports reading procedural terms with their historically “transplanted” meaning where the Rules were modeled on prior regimes; the historical authorities and the Advisory Committee’s reliance on a California model (e.g., Palace Hardware) indicate that courts retained power to set aside voluntary dismissals on proper showings. This narrow reading preserves institutional legitimacy by aligning the Federal Rules with their text and historical understanding without expanding Article III jurisdiction or altering Rule 41’s self-executing operation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and the inclusion of “proceeding” must be given independent textual effect beyond court-entered judgments or orders. A Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice is self-executing and terminates the case in federal court; in ordinary legal usage and historical remedial practice, such a termination is a “final … proceeding” from which a court may grant limited post-termination relief in extraordinary circumstances, consistent with Rule 60(b)’s preservation of equitable mechanisms and its abolition of older writs and bills in favor of this rule. The “without prejudice” label does not defeat finality for Rule 60(b) purposes because the relevant question is whether the federal proceeding has ended, not whether refiling is theoretically possible. Consistent with the Court’s approach to “transplanted” legal terms carrying their historical meaning, see Hall v. Hall, the better reading is that Rule 60(b) reaches voluntary dismissals that finally conclude the federal proceeding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Rule 60(b) by its terms reaches relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal is a docketed act that terminates the federal case—functionally final as to the court’s involvement—even if it is without prejudice and involves no judicial order. Reading “proceeding” to exclude such a case-terminating dismissal risks rendering that word largely redundant with “judgment” and “order,” contrary to ordinary textualist principles. Historical practice and the “transplanted term” principle support that understanding: where the Rules adopt broad remedial language, courts traditionally could set aside voluntary nonsuits/dismissals in appropriate circumstances, and Hall v. Hall counsels against silently reimagining the meaning of an adopted term. Consistent with that, Kokkonen’s dicta and decisions like Williams v. Frey recognize that a voluntary dismissal may be treated as a “proceeding” subject to Rule 60(b), allowing limited, consequence-sensitive reopening in extraordinary cases without broadly undermining Rule 41’s self-executing mechanism.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief not only from a final “judgment” or “order,” but also from a final “proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal is a party-initiated act that conclusively terminates the federal case in that court. Interpreting “proceeding” to include such self-executing dismissals aligns with the Court’s interpretive principle that transplanted procedural terms carry their historical meaning, see Hall v. Hall, and with historical practice recognizing courts’ power to set aside voluntary dismissals in extraordinary circumstances. Denying Rule 60(b) relief categorically would unnecessarily foreclose equitable remedies where vulnerable litigants are misled by procedural traps or later developments (including jurisdictional shifts discussed in Badgerow) make the dismissal’s consequences unjust, even though the plaintiff may theoretically refile. The better reading preserves district courts’ broad remedial authority to reopen on “just terms” when Rule 60(b)’s stringent standards are met, without undermining Rule 41’s ordinary operation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal is a case-terminating procedural act that ends the federal litigation, making it naturally describable as a “final … proceeding” even absent a judicial “order.” Reading “proceeding” to include such self-executing dismissals best preserves statutory coherence and workability: it allows courts to correct extraordinary mistakes or inequities without forcing duplicative refilings, while leaving Rule 41’s self-executing feature intact and confining relief to Rule 60(b)’s demanding standards. The historical model for Rule 60(b) and pre-Rules practice reinforce that understanding, and under Hall v. Hall’s “transplanted term” principle, the Rules’ adoption of a term modeled on prior remedial regimes presumptively carries forward its established meaning—including the ability to set aside voluntary dismissals in appropriate circumstances. Respondent’s view would treat “proceeding” as surplusage and improperly make judicial action a prerequisite that the text does not impose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal—though self-executing and without judicial action—nevertheless ends the case in federal court and thus qualifies as a “final … proceeding” in ordinary legal usage. Reading “proceeding” to exclude party-initiated steps would unnaturally narrow the text, especially given the Rules’ broader use of “proceedings” to include party-driven acts (e.g., Rules 37(b)(2)(A)(iv), 41(d), 62(a)). And under the transplanted-term canon applied in Hall v. Hall, where a Rule term is borrowed from earlier regimes, we presume it carries its established meaning; historical practice included courts’ power to set aside voluntary nonsuits/dismissals in appropriate circumstances. This interpretation respects separation of powers by adhering to the Rules’ enacted text rather than inventing a jurisdictional carveout not found in Rule 60(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) makes a plaintiff’s notice of dismissal self-executing and effective upon filing, without any judicial act; that structure strongly suggests it is not a “final judgment” or “final order” within Rule 60(b), and reading “final … proceeding” to require at least some judicial determination avoids converting Rule 60(b) into a general supervisory power over party-initiated case terminations. Although petitioner invokes history and the “transplanted term” principle discussed in Hall v. Hall, the better institutional and workability reading is that Rule 60(b) targets relief from judicially entered final dispositions, while a dismissal without prejudice leaves the plaintiff free to refile and thus lacks the kind of finality Rule 60(b) presupposes. That approach also respects judicial restraint and clear rule-based lines: once a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice is filed, the case is terminated and the district court lacks a continuing proceeding to “reopen” under Rule 60(b). Any equitable concerns arising from later developments (e.g., Badgerow) are better addressed through refiling or other available avenues rather than expanding Rule 60(b)’s scope beyond its text and structure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal is a case-terminating procedural act that ends the action in federal court upon filing, making it “final” in the ordinary sense relevant to reopening. Reading “proceeding” to exclude self-executing dismissals would drain the word of independent meaning and create an odd asymmetry with Rule 41(a)(1)(B), which gives a notice dismissal adjudicative effect in specified circumstances even absent a court order. Consistent with the interpretive principle that transplanted procedural terms carry their historical remedial content, pre-Federal Rules practice recognized authority to set aside voluntary nonsuits/dismissals on motion in appropriate circumstances, supporting that a voluntary dismissal can be the kind of “proceeding” Rule 60(b) reaches. Precedent does not compel the contrary, and this reading best harmonizes Rules 41 and 60 while preserving Rule 60(b)’s narrow, equitable function.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of dismissal—though self-executing and without judicial involvement—conclusively terminates the federal case and thus functions as a “final … proceeding” for purposes of post-termination relief. Reading “proceeding” to carry its historically broader, remedial meaning is consistent with this Court’s interpretive approach to transplanted legal terms, see Hall v. Hall, and avoids creating a procedural trap where litigants who dismiss to pursue arbitration (or for other case-management reasons) lose any ability to seek equitable relief when extraordinary circumstances arise. Limiting Rule 60(b) to court-entered judgments/orders would elevate form over practical consequences and undermine procedural fairness by foreclosing correction of serious irregularities solely because the termination occurred via a party notice rather than a court order. This construction still preserves Rule 41’s self-executing effect and finality interests because Rule 60(b) remains an extraordinary remedy, not an invitation to relitigate, and can be applied on “just terms” in the rare case warranting reopening.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff’s unilateral voluntary dismissal without prejudice under Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) qualifies as a “final judgment, order, or proceeding” that a federal district court may reopen under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b) (relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding”) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i) (plaintiff’s notice of voluntary dismissal without a court order).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: A Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) voluntary dismissal without prejudice is at least a “final ... proceeding” within the meaning of Rule 60(b) because it terminates the federal case and is a formal, case-ending step taken in court; historically, the term “proceeding” was used broadly to include any step in the progress of a civil action from commencement to termination, including dismissals initiated by the plaintiff. Petitioner argues that allowing Rule 60(b) relief fits the rule’s equitable purpose (to prevent injustice on just terms) and is especially appropriate where post-dismissal developments (including intervening Supreme Court law affecting jurisdiction over FAA-related proceedings, referenced as Badgerow) and unusual arbitral irregularities make reopening necessary to accomplish justice. Petitioner also relies on the existence of a circuit split and contends the contrary view improperly elevates form (no court order) over substance (a final termination of the case).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief only from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) dismissal without prejudice is none of these because it is self-executing, requires no judicial act, produces no court order, and is not sufficiently ‘final’ in the sense relevant to Rule 60(b) given that it leaves the plaintiff free to refile. Respondent argues the Tenth Circuit correctly held that once the plaintiff filed the notice of dismissal, the district court lacked jurisdiction to reopen because there was nothing judicial to set aside; any remedy lies in filing a new action (subject to defenses like limitations), not in resurrecting a voluntarily abandoned case. Respondent further emphasizes the question is narrow and rarely arises, and that expanding Rule 60(b) to cover non-prejudicial voluntary dismissals would create procedural uncertainty and undermine the clean, automatic effect of Rule 41(a)(1).
key_precedents: Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. ___ (2022) (referenced as intervening Supreme Court law affecting FAA jurisdiction)
Volt Information Sciences, Inc. v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior Univ., 489 U.S. 468 (1989) (parties’ freedom to structure arbitration procedures)
Stolt-Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp., 559 U.S. 662 (2010) (arbitrator’s powers derive from the parties’ agreement)
Mid Atl. Cap. Corp. v. Bien, 956 F.3d 1182 (10th Cir. 2020) (contracting for reasoned awards / arbitration procedure principles)
Hall v. Hall, 584 U.S. 73 (2018) (interpretive principle about transplanted legal terms carrying prior meaning)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is structural and institutional: Rule 41(a)(1) is self-executing and prized for certainty, and letting Rule 60(b) reach a unilateral notice could invite post hoc revival. But that concern doesn’t overcome the text: Rule 60(b) expressly extends beyond “judgment” and “order” to a “final … proceeding,” and as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas argue, treating the case-terminating notice as a final proceeding gives that residual term independent work without unsettling Rule 41’s automatic effect. Hall v. Hall reinforces the minimalist, text-bound route—give the transplanted term “proceeding” its established meaning—while leaving for later cases what kinds of Rule 41 dismissals and what showings satisfy Rule 60(b)’s narrow, discretionary gates. On this framing, Rule 41’s certainty remains the default; Rule 60(b) is merely an exceptional safety valve, not an invitation to routine resurrection.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is structural: Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) is self-executing and designed to provide certainty, so Rule 60(b) relief might look like an impermissible resurrection of a case ended without any court act. But that argument cannot overcome Rule 60(b)’s text, which extends beyond “judgment” and “order” to a “final … proceeding,” and Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly emphasize that a docketed notice that terminates the action leaves nothing pending and is “final” in the sense opposite of interlocutory. Hall v. Hall reinforces our ordinary interpretive approach: transplanted legal terms carry their settled meaning, and historically “proceeding” was broad enough to encompass formal steps through termination, so excluding a case-ending voluntary dismissal would improperly read that residual term out of the Rule. Any concern about eroding Rule 41’s certainty is answered by Rule 60(b)’s own strict limits (grounds, timeliness, and discretionary relief on “just terms”), which preserve Rule 41’s automatic effect while allowing exceptional correction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas have the best petitioner-side point: “proceeding” must add something beyond “judgment” and “order,” and historically it can be capacious. But that does not answer the limiting modifier “final” in Rule 60(b) when paired with Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i)’s deliberate design—an automatic, nonprejudicial, freely refileable termination that divests the court without any court-controlled disposition to relieve from. Justice Barrett’s appeal to Hall v. Hall’s “transplanted term” principle does not move me because Hall concerned appealability of judicially managed case segments, not whether Rule 60(b) supplies power to undo a party’s unilateral abandonment; importing a broad abstract meaning here undermines Rule 41’s core practical function of certainty and invites strategic resurrection. The equitable concerns raised by Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson (limitations, Badgerow-like forum loss) are real, but under a textual and structural reading they cannot expand Rule 60(b) into a backdoor to restore jurisdiction after a self-executing dismissal where the Rules channel plaintiffs to refiling subject to ordinary defenses.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that Rule 41(a)(1) is meant to be self-executing and certain, and that letting Rule 60(b) in could invite “resurrection”—does not overcome Rule 60(b)’s text, which expressly reaches a “final … proceeding” in addition to a “judgment” or “order.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading “proceeding” to exclude the docketed, case-terminating notice effectively drains that word of independent meaning, while Rule 60(b)’s narrow grounds, strict timeliness, and discretionary “just terms” adequately preserve Rule 41’s default certainty and guard against routine relitigation. Justice Gorsuch’s historical/transplanted-term point (echoed by Justice Thomas) further undercuts the respondent’s premise that judicial issuance is required: the Rules’ structure can remain self-executing while still permitting exceptional relief from the case-ending act. On my pragmatic approach, an absolute bar risks turning a procedural dismissal into an access-to-justice trap when refiling is practically unavailable, without a textual necessity to do so.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is structural and institutional: Rule 41(a)(1) is designed to be self-executing and certain, and a Rule 60(b) back-end could invite resurrection of abandoned cases. But that concern cannot override Rule 60(b)’s text, which extends to a “final … proceeding,” and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize—a filed notice that terminates the action on the docket is “final” in the only sense the Rule’s structure requires (nothing remains pending), even if the dismissal is without prejudice. Hall v. Hall, invoked by multiple colleagues, strengthens the textual inference that “proceeding” is a transplanted, capacious term that must do work beyond “judgment” and “order,” rather than being artificially confined to court-entered dispositions. The certainty interests Alito and Kavanaugh identify are better accommodated by insisting on Rule 60(b)’s narrow grounds, timeliness, and discretionary “just terms,” not by adopting an atextual categorical bar that drains “proceeding” of independent meaning.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest contention—that Rule 60(b) presupposes a court-entered judgment or order and that allowing relief from a unilateral Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice would erode Rule 41’s certainty—runs into the enacted text: Rule 60(b) extends to a “final … proceeding,” and reading “proceeding” to require judicial action largely collapses it into “judgment” and “order.” Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas persuasively ground “proceeding” in its historically capacious, transplanted meaning (reinforced by Hall v. Hall’s interpretive approach), which comfortably includes a formal, docketed, case-terminating notice that leaves nothing pending and is thus “final” in the interlocutory-versus-terminal sense. Justice Kavanaugh’s finality concerns are real but are addressed by Rule 60(b)’s own limiting architecture—enumerated grounds, timeliness, and relief only on “just terms”—so recognizing availability here does not rewrite Rule 41’s self-executing effect but simply identifies what kind of terminal act Rule 60(b) may, in exceptional cases, reach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point that “proceeding” must do independent work is the most serious argument for petitioner, but I remain unpersuaded that it requires treating a unilateral Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice as a “final … proceeding” subject to Rule 60(b) relief. Even accepting Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s broad, historically rooted account of “proceeding” (and the Hall v. Hall transplanted-term methodology), the institutional and structural fit matters: Rule 60(b) presupposes relief from a court-controlled termination (judgment/order or their functional equivalent), whereas a self-executing notice is designed to end the court’s involvement and provide bright-line certainty and jurisdictional closure. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s equity concerns (time bars, post-Badgerow effects) are real but case-specific; they do not justify expanding Rule 60(b) into a mechanism to unwind a party’s voluntary, freely refileable dismissal in a way that would predictably invite routine “resurrection” motions and erode Rule 41’s workmanlike finality.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest respondent point: Rule 41(a)(1) is self-executing and designed for certainty, and Rule 60(b) supposedly presupposes a court-entered judgment or order to unwind. But that structural concern cannot override Rule 60(b)’s text, which expressly reaches a “final … proceeding,” and—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s historical-textual account—a docketed notice that terminates the action is final in the relevant sense (nothing remains pending), even if it is without prejudice. Hall v. Hall, as several colleagues note, supports giving “proceeding” its established, capacious meaning rather than collapsing it into “judgment” and “order,” which would make the residual term largely superfluous. The certainty interest is protected by Rule 60(b)’s narrow grounds, timeliness limits, and discretionary “just terms,” so recognizing availability does not convert Rule 60(b) into a general license to undo voluntary dismissals.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) is self-executing and certainty would be undermined if a party can later “resurrect” a dismissed case—has real force, but it does not fit the text of Rule 60(b), which extends beyond “judgment” and “order” to a “final … proceeding.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the notice is a formal, docketed, case-terminating step that leaves nothing pending, so it is “final” in the opposite-of-interlocutory sense even if without prejudice, and excluding it would largely drain “proceeding” of independent meaning. On my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the certainty concern is adequately handled by Rule 60(b)’s narrow grounds, strict timing, and “just terms,” which preserve Rule 41’s ordinary automaticity while preventing procedural traps where refiling is practically foreclosed. Hall v. Hall’s transplanted-term method (invoked by several colleagues) reinforces that we should not artificially confine “proceeding” to judge-entered acts when the Rules chose a broader term with established scope.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(b) authorizes relief from a “final judgment, order, or proceeding,” and a Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) notice of voluntary dismissal, though self-executing and without prejudice, is still a case-terminating “proceeding” in the ordinary and historically settled sense of that transplanted term. Hall’s interpretive approach, the better reading gives “proceeding” independent work beyond “judgment” and “order,” allowing limited reopening where equity requires while leaving Rule 41(a)(1)’s automatic dismissal effect intact absent a granted Rule 60(b) motion.
